title: Matplotlib Pie Charts, Labels and Exploded Slices
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and core concepts of Matplotlib Pie Charts, Labels and Exploded Slices.
Select suitable Python structures or library operations for the task.

understand.concept: A pie chart represents parts of a whole using wedges whose sizes are proportional to non-negative values. Labels identify categories, startangle rotates the chart, explode offsets selected wedges, and autopct formats percentage labels. Pie charts are most useful for a small number of categories that sum to a meaningful whole.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct labeling and interpretation prevent misleading part-to-whole comparisons.
understand.analogy: Choose the data structure or chart that matches the information being represented; visual similarity does not mean two structures have identical behavior.
understand.summary: Matplotlib Pie Charts, Labels and Exploded Slices adds a focused capability to the Python curriculum.

explain.narrative: Read the concept, run each example in order, inspect the returned values and figure objects, and compare the result with the stated expectation. The examples use deterministic data and a non-interactive Matplotlib backend so they can be validated in automation.

examples.title: Create labeled pie wedges
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
wedges, texts = ax.pie([3, 1], labels=['A', 'B'])
print(len(wedges), [t.get_text() for t in texts])
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Each value creates one wedge and each supplied label names it.

examples.title: Display percentage labels
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
wedges, texts, auto = ax.pie([1, 1], autopct='%1.0f%%')
print([t.get_text() for t in auto])
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: autopct formats the percentage represented by each wedge.

examples.title: Rotate the first wedge
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
wedges, _ = ax.pie([1, 1], startangle=90)
print(round(wedges[0].theta1))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: startangle controls the initial orientation of the pie.

examples.title: Explode one category
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
wedges, _ = ax.pie([2, 3], explode=[0.1, 0])
print(wedges[0].center != wedges[1].center)
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A non-zero explode value offsets that wedge from the center.

examples.title: Validate values before plotting
examples.code:
values = [4, 6, 0]
valid = all(v >= 0 for v in values) and sum(values) > 0
print(valid, sum(values))
examples.explanation: Pie values should be non-negative and have a positive total.

questions.prompt: What does a pie wedge represent?
questions.answer: A category's share of the whole
options: A category's share of the whole

questions.prompt: Which input is unsuitable for a meaningful pie chart?
questions.explanation: Negative values cannot represent non-negative shares of a whole.

questions.prompt: When are pie charts most readable?
